nameStory: The swamp beacon gets its name from its bright orange or yellow club-shaped cap that glows like a tiny beacon among the dark, soggy vegetation of wetlands. The scientific name 'Mitrula' comes from the Latin word for a ceremonial cap or headdress, referring to the distinctive dome-shaped top. Like a lighthouse guiding ships, these little fungi guide the eyes of nature explorers through murky swampland.
description: Swamp beacon is a small, distinctive fungus that looks like a tiny orange or yellow club poking up from wet ground. The fruiting body has a smooth, rounded cap on top of a pale, slender stem, typically reaching just 1-2 inches tall. This little fungus belongs to a group called cup fungi, though it doesn't look cup-like at all. You'll spot these bright beacons dotting boggy areas and wet woodlands throughout New England.

idTips.label: Club-shaped fruiting body
idTips.description: The entire mushroom looks like a small orange or yellow club or paddle, with a smooth, rounded head that feels slightly rubbery to the touch

idTips.label: Bright orange-yellow color
idTips.description: The cap glows bright orange, yellow, or orange-red, creating a striking contrast against dark soil and green moss

idTips.label: Pale stem
idTips.description: The stem is much paler than the cap, often whitish or cream-colored, and feels firm but slightly flexible when gently pressed

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Rarely grows taller than 2 inches, making it easy to overlook until the bright color catches your eye

idTips.label: Smooth, waxy texture
idTips.description: The cap surface is completely smooth and has a slightly waxy or rubbery feel, never rough or scaly

idTips.label: Wetland habitat
idTips.description: Always found in very wet areas - if your feet aren't getting damp, you're not in swamp beacon territory

habitat: Swamp beacons thrive in permanently wet or boggy areas including sphagnum bogs, wet meadows, swamps, and the soggy edges of ponds and streams. They grow directly from wet soil, often among mosses, sedges, and other wetland plants. In New England, look for them in places where water sits on the surface for much of the year, from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Young fruiting bodies begin emerging in late spring as soil warms, appearing as tiny bright dots in wet areas. Fresh specimens have the most vibrant coloring during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for swamp beacons, with mature fruiting bodies most abundant during warm, humid weather. The bright colors are most striking against lush green summer vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Fruiting continues into early fall, though specimens may appear more weathered and faded. Late season finds can help distinguish this species from spring-only lookalikes.
seasonality.winter: No visible fruiting bodies present above ground, though the fungal network remains active in the soil beneath ice and snow.

funFact: Despite being called a beacon, this tiny fungus actually glows brightest on the gloomiest days - its vibrant orange color appears most saturated under the overcast skies that are perfect for mushroom hunting, making it nature's own mood ring for cloudy weather.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small orange coral fungi, but swamp beacon is always a single simple club shape, never branched like coral. Remember: 'One club in the bog, coral branches on logs' - swamp beacon grows from wet soil while coral fungi typically grow on decaying wood.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'swamp beacon' is sometimes applied to different Mitrula species, creating confusion among field guides. Some sources use this common name for the closely related Mitrula paludosa, so when sharing finds with other naturalists, it's helpful to mention the scientific name Mitrula elegans to be specific.
compareHints: Swamp beacon (Mitrula elegans) is typically more vibrantly colored than its close relative Mitrula paludosa, showing brighter oranges and yellows versus the more subdued orange-brown tones of M. paludosa. Mitrula elegans also tends to have a more distinctly club-shaped head, while M. paludosa can appear more irregularly rounded. Both require microscopic examination of spores for definitive identification, but the brighter coloration of M. elegans is a good field clue.
